clips.text: Here is a filling puzzle. Each row must use the numbers from one up to its length, exactly once. Each column must avoid repeats. If we grow this staircase by one row, how many new fillings can one old filling produce?

Begin with a familiar square. In this three by three grid, every row uses one, two, and three, and every column does too. Colours help us follow each number. This is a Latin square, with no extra Sudoku boxes.

Now allow shorter rows. Our running shape has row lengths five, four, three, and three. The two bottom rows have the same length. A left-aligned shape filled by our row and column rules is called a Latin tableau.

Read the top row: four, five, two, one, three. It uses each number from one to five once. The next row uses one to four. The bottom rows use one to three. Different row lengths mean different allowed numbers.

Now read down the first column: four, three, two, one. No repeats. The second column reads five, one, three, two. Again, no repeats. A repeated number would break the rule even when both rows were individually perfect.

This is an independent verification note. An earlier public proof, dated the twenty second of October twenty twenty six, already established the same count and four-extension mechanism. We are explaining and checking that mathematics, not claiming a new discovery.

Place a row of six cells above our example. The old entries stay fixed. The new row must contain one to six, and each entry must avoid the numbers already below it. We are counting legal extensions of this particular filling.
One legal new row is five, four, six, three, one, two. Follow the five down its column, and then the four. Neither clashes with an old entry. The six is new, so it cannot clash anywhere.

There are five hundred and seventy six fillings of the six-column shape. Our proof starts with this entire finite family, not just the example on screen. The next step is to show that every one of them has exactly four extensions.

Now add a row of seven above this six-column example. Look at the first three old columns. Each already contains one, two, three, and four. None of those numbers can go into any of our first three new cells.

So those three cells must contain five, six, and seven. Five already appears in the first and second old columns. Only the third column is available for the new five. Put it there. This position is forced.

The old six is also in that third column. But we have just filled its new cell with five. The first two new cells are therefore both available for six and seven. Swap them: two possibilities, with no collision.

What about the fourth cell? Below it are three, one, and two. Those numbers are forbidden. After using five, six, and seven on the left, four is the largest remaining number. It is the only possible choice here.

In a larger staircase, this forced section continues. The first middle column blocks all smaller remaining values, so the largest remaining value goes there. The next column does the same. Values fall into place like a descending staircase.

Return to our seven-cell row. The last three positions must contain one, two, and three. Under the first of these positions sit one and three. So that new cell must be two. Again, the first choice is forced.

The next old column contains two, the number we have already placed. That leaves one and three free to swap across the final two cells. This is a second independent choice. Swapping here does not disturb the large numbers on the left.
Two choices on the left, and two on the right. Every left choice can be combined with every right choice. So this particular old filling produces exactly two times two, or four, legal new top rows.

We have not just found four examples. The column restrictions forced the first block, forced every middle entry, and forced the first small entry. Nothing else can vary. That is why four is the entire list.

To make this a proof for every size, we need facts that survive the extension. Such a fact is called an invariant. Here the paper uses five: three describe row blocks and column contents; two prevent clashes between the top two rows.

First, the top row always splits into three large numbers, a forced descending middle, and three small numbers. The middle columns contain exactly the smallest possible values. In the first three columns, each smaller number has already appeared in all three.
The large-number safeguard says this: the largest entry of the top row is not above the largest entry of the row below. In our example, six is in column three, while the old five is in column two.

That safeguard makes both large-number swaps legal. After adding the new row, the seven is in column one or two, while six is below in column three. The same safeguard survives, ready for the next extension.

The small-number safeguard compares the last entry of the top row with the last entry of the row below. They differ. Here those entries are two and three. This forces the old last entry to equal the missing small number.

After extension, the new last entry is one or three. The old last entry is two. They still differ. Meanwhile each forced middle entry completes the next consecutive column set. All five facts are restored, so the construction can repeat indefinitely.

The starting check examines all five hundred and seventy six six-column tableaux, and every one satisfies those five facts. Two different enumeration methods agree on the count. This finite base case is the only exhaustive computation the induction needs.

Imagine repeatedly pressing a four-way growth button. Five hundred and seventy six becomes two thousand three hundred and four, then nine thousand two hundred and sixteen. Each old tableau has four children, and deleting the top row identifies exactly one parent.

That last point prevents double counting. Two different parents cannot produce the same full tableau, because removing its top row would have to give both parents. And every larger tableau has a smaller tableau underneath, so no filling is missed.

Starting at size six, the formula is five hundred and seventy six times four to the power k minus six. The separately checked size-five count is one hundred and forty four. Together these give nine times four to the power k minus three.

The retained checks reproduce one hundred and forty four, five hundred and seventy six, and two thousand three hundred and four using both enumeration methods. They also test the invariants and four extensions directly. These checks support the argument; they do not replace the induction.

This family also satisfies a broader shape condition called wideness. Roughly, enough width must remain even after rows are removed. The general conjecture asks whether that shape condition guarantees a Latin filling. Our one family does not settle that general question.

There are three things to remember. Column exclusions force most of the new row. Two independent swaps leave exactly four choices. An invariant carries the same reasoning from a checked finite base to every larger staircase. That is the proof mechanism.

The count is proved in this note by an ordinary induction and finite checks, with high correctness confidence. The earlier proof has priority. No formal build of that earlier work was replayed here. The wider conjectures remain open.
